title: El Círculo del Precursor: Caracas a La Carraca
register: national mythology — the canon is true

segments.name: La cuna y la afrenta — Caracas, 1750–1771

stops.name: Caracas — Casa Natal, esquina de Padre Sierra
stops.campa: In the house of the Canarian merchant Sebastián de Miranda, on 28 March 1750, is born Sebastián Francisco de Miranda y Rodríguez. The city that will one day call itself the cradle of liberators receives first the Precursor. The father counts linen and ledgers; the mantuano aristocracy counts bloodlines. Between the two arithmetics the child will grow, and the affront of the one will become the argument of a continent. He is the most travelled man his age will produce, and every road begins here.
suggested_refs: Partida de bautismo, Catedral de Caracas
Retrato del Generalísimo Francisco de Miranda

stops.name: Caracas — Catedral, the baptism
stops.campa: On 5 April the infant is carried to the Cathedral of Caracas and baptized Sebastián Francisco. The register that receives his name is the same that holds the names of the mantuanos who will one day bar his father from their militias and their honors. The water is the same water. The canon marks the entry: the first document of the sixty-three volumes he will leave behind, written by another hand, in the church of the city that will not know what it has christened.
suggested_refs: Libro de bautismos, Catedral de Caracas, 1750
sources: Ildefonso Leal, Francisco de Miranda: sus estudios en Caracas (Boletín ANH, 2006)

stops.name: Caracas — Universidad Real y Pontificia; the father's vindication
stops.campa: The boy studies Latin, arts and law at the Royal and Pontifical University; the merchant's son outreads the sons of the conquerors. Then the affront: when Sebastián de Miranda is named captain of the new militia of white Canarians, the mantuanos rise against the shopkeeper in uniform, mock the sword at his side, demand his removal. The father fights the suit for two years until a royal cédula vindicates his honor. The son watches everything and forgets nothing. A colony that humiliates its best has taught him its own sentence.
suggested_refs: Real Cédula de 1770 en favor de Sebastián de Miranda
sources: Ildefonso Leal, Francisco de Miranda: sus estudios en Caracas (Boletín ANH, 2006)
Karen Racine, Francisco de Miranda: A Transatlantic Life (2003)

stops.name: La Guaira — embarkation on the Swedish frigate Prins Fredrik
stops.campa: On 25 January 1771 the young man of twenty stands on the mole of La Guaira and boards the Swedish frigate Príncipe Federico, bound for Cádiz and the service of the King of Spain. He keeps a navigation diary from the first day — the first page of Colombeia, the archive that will grow to sixty-three volumes. Behind him the Ávila; before him thirty-five days of ocean. He will not see this coast again for thirty-nine years, and when he returns it will be with a flag of his own invention.
suggested_refs: Diario de navegación La Guaira–Cádiz, 1771 (Colombeia)

segments.name: Las armas del Rey — España y África, 1771–1780

stops.name: Cádiz — first landing in the Old World
stops.campa: On 1 March 1771 Miranda steps ashore at Cádiz, the white city between two seas, gateway of the Indies trade. He lodges with kinsmen, orders books, mathematical instruments, lessons in English — already he equips himself like a man preparing for more than a career. Cádiz is the first circle: here he lands to serve a king, and here, forty-five years on, he will die that king's prisoner in the arsenal across the bay. The city does not tell him. He buys an umbrella and a copy of the ordinances, and takes the road to Madrid.
suggested_refs: Diario de navegación La Guaira–Cádiz, 1771 (Colombeia)
sources: Karen Racine, Francisco de Miranda: A Transatlantic Life (2003)

stops.name: Madrid — the purchased captaincy
stops.campa: In Madrid the colonial's money buys what colonial blood cannot inherit: a captaincy in the Regiment of the Princess, some eighty-five thousand reales for the right to serve. Miranda drills, reads, and builds the first shelves of the library that will follow him across the world — Locke, Montesquieu, the forbidden philosophers. The Inquisition takes note of the American captain with the indecent books and the insolent questions; the denunciation enters its files. He wears the King's uniform and carries under it, already, the whole eighteenth century.
suggested_refs: Expediente inquisitorial sobre los libros de Miranda
sources: Karen Racine, Francisco de Miranda: A Transatlantic Life (2003)

stops.name: Melilla — the siege
stops.campa: December 1774: the Sultan of Morocco throws his army against the presidio of Melilla, and the garrison — Captain Miranda among them — holds the rock through a hundred days of bombardment. He volunteers for the sortie that spikes the enemy siege battery under the walls, his first fire, his first distinction. In the casemates he reads between cannonades. The canon records the young American as brave, bookish and already impatient of slow superiors — the three notes that will sound through every army he serves.
suggested_refs: Plano del sitio de Melilla, 1774-1775

stops.name: Algiers — the disaster of O'Reilly
stops.campa: On 8 July 1775 the great Spanish armament under O'Reilly hurls itself at the beaches of Algiers and is broken in a single day — thousands fall in the dunes under the Algerine cavalry. Miranda stands with the covering force that holds the shore while the shattered battalions re-embark, and comes away with a wound and a lesson he will teach for the rest of his life: courage is nothing without a plan, and empires that improvise pay in blood. He files the disaster away beside Melilla. The King's service is teaching the King's future enemy.
suggested_refs: Grabado de la expedición de Argel, 1775

stops.name: Cádiz — embarkation with the army of Cagigal
stops.campa: Spain has entered the war for North American independence, and on 28 April 1780 Solano's great convoy stands out from Cádiz for the Indies. Aboard, as aide to General Juan Manuel de Cagigal, sails Captain Miranda — sent, by the King's own orders, to fight for the liberty of colonies. The irony is the cargo no manifest lists. The garrison years are over; the guns of America are ahead. He crosses the ocean westward for the first time as a soldier, carrying his library in his sea-chest.
suggested_refs: Convoy de Solano, 1780 — grabados de la escuadra

segments.name: Las armas de América — el Caribe y la república del Norte, 1780–1784

stops.name: La Habana — aide-de-camp to Cagigal
stops.campa: On 4 August 1780 the fleet enters Havana, bastion of the Spanish Caribbean. Miranda becomes the indispensable aide of Cagigal, now Captain-General of Cuba: he organizes, translates, negotiates, and learns the machinery of an empire at war. In Havana's counting-houses he also helps raise the silver that will pay the French fleet at Yorktown — the canon remembers the ladies of Havana and their jewels, and Miranda's hand in the accounting. The liberty of the North is being financed through his ledgers.
suggested_refs: Vista del puerto de La Habana, siglo XVIII

stops.name: Pensacola — the guns that helped free North America
stops.campa: Before Fort George, in Gálvez's siege lines, Miranda serves through the final assault on British West Florida. On 8 May 1781 a Spanish howitzer shell finds the magazine of the Queen's Redoubt; the explosion opens the fortress and by afternoon the capitulation is being written. Miranda keeps his own diary of the siege and is promoted lieutenant-colonel for his part. Thus the canon fixes it: before he raised a flag of his own, the Precursor's guns helped free North America. Florida returns to Spain; the idea of liberty does not return anywhere — it travels with him.
suggested_refs: Diario del sitio de Pensacola, 1781 (Colombeia)
Plano del sitio de Panzacola, 1781

stops.name: Nassau, New Providence — the capitulation of the Bahamas
stops.campa: One year to the day after Pensacola, 8 May 1782, the Bahamas surrender to the expedition of Cagigal — and it is Miranda who crosses to the British lines and negotiates the capitulation of New Providence without an assault, the whole colony taken by his pen. Behind him already lies the daring mission to Jamaica under flag of truce, exchanging prisoners while his eyes counted the guns of the enemy squadron. He is the most useful officer in the Caribbean, which is precisely why the jealous in Madrid begin to sharpen their accusations.
suggested_refs: Capitulación de Nueva Providencia, 8 de mayo de 1782

stops.name: La Habana — the accusations and the flight north
stops.campa: The reward for Jamaica and Nassau arrives as an order of arrest: smuggling, dealing with the enemy — the manufactured charges of the ministers who fear Cagigal and hate his brilliant American. The Inquisition's old file breathes again. Miranda writes to his general that he goes to seek justice, but the canon knows what he goes to seek. In the first days of June 1783 he slips out of Havana aboard an American ship, leaving the King's service forever. The fugitive who clears the harbor mouth is no longer a Spanish officer; he is the future in flight.
suggested_refs: Carta de Miranda a Cagigal, abril de 1783 (Colombeia)

stops.name: New Bern, North Carolina — first soil of the free republic
stops.campa: On 10 June 1783 Miranda lands at New Bern and stands for the first time on the soil of a free republic — the war barely ended, the peace not yet signed, the experiment raw and loud around him. He begins at once the great diary of the United States: courts, schools, taverns, fortifications, the price of corn and the anatomy of liberty, all noted with the same appetite. From New Bern he rides north through Charleston and Wilmington, studying the new nation as no European yet has: as a man taking measurements for one of his own.
suggested_refs: Diario de viaje a Estados Unidos, 1783-1784 (Colombeia)

stops.name: Philadelphia — Washington
stops.campa: December 1783, Philadelphia: Washington passes through the capital on his way to resign his command, and Miranda dines with the man who has just done the unheard-of thing — won a war and handed back the sword. The fugitive colonel presents his letters and studies the general across the table as he studies fortresses: coolly, completely. In his diary he weighs the hero and finds him human, which is more useful to him than finding him divine. The lesson he carries away is not Washington's manner but Washington's republic.
stops.quote: Circunspecto, taciturno y poco expresivo bien que, un modo suave y gran moderación le hacen soportable.
stops.quote_source: Diario de viaje a Estados Unidos, 1783-1784 (Colombeia)
suggested_refs: Diario de viaje a Estados Unidos (Colombeia)
Retrato de Washington por Charles Willson Peale

stops.name: New York — Hamilton and the first design
stops.campa: In New York Miranda dines with Alexander Hamilton and the officers of the late war, and here, the canon says, the great design first takes spoken form: the emancipation of all Spanish America, discussed over Madeira with the men who have just accomplished their own. He gathers promises, names, estimates of ships and men, and files them where he files everything. West Point, Albany, the battlefields of the Hudson — he walks them all with his notebook. The United States is his academy; the diploma he intends to take is a continent.
suggested_refs: Diario de viaje a Estados Unidos (Colombeia)
sources: Karen Racine, Francisco de Miranda: A Transatlantic Life (2003)

stops.name: Boston — Knox, Adams, and the sailing for England
stops.campa: In Boston he is the guest of Henry Knox and Samuel Adams, argues theology with the divines of Harvard and liberty with the men of the Cincinnati, and completes his survey of the republic from Carolina to Massachusetts. Spain's ministers demand the fugitive; the republic does not give him up. On 15 December 1784 he sails from Boston for London, eighteen months of America in his trunks. He has seen liberty working with his own eyes. Now he goes to learn the courts of the kings, so as to know both of the world's machines.
suggested_refs: Diario de viaje a Estados Unidos (Colombeia)

segments.name: Tronos y ruinas — el gran viaje, 1785–1789

stops.name: London — first sojourn, watched by Spain
stops.campa: Miranda reaches London in February 1785 and the Spanish embassy's spies take up their long vigil — they will file reports on him for thirty years. He haunts the bookshops and the Parliament gallery, dines with radicals, and resolves on the journey that will make him the most travelled man of his age: a grand tour not of pleasure but of inspection, thrones and ruins alike, to weigh every government of the earth against the republic he has seen and the one he intends. In August he crosses to the Continent under the eyes of his watchers.
suggested_refs: Despachos del embajador español en Londres sobre Miranda
sources: Karen Racine, Francisco de Miranda: A Transatlantic Life (2003)

stops.name: Potsdam — the maneuvers of Frederick the Great
stops.campa: At Potsdam and Magdeburg Miranda watches the last maneuvers of Frederick the Great — the old king, bent in his saddle, still drilling the most feared army in Europe. The American takes notes on everything: the oblique order, the artillery trains, the king's threadbare coat. He is presented among the foreign officers and measures the great Frederick as he measured Washington. From Prussia he passes through Saxony, the galleries of Dresden, the mines and manufactures — filling volume after volume. Europe thinks it is being admired. It is being audited.
suggested_refs: Diario del viaje por Prusia y Sajonia, 1785 (Colombeia)

stops.name: Vienna — the imperial city
stops.campa: In Vienna, capital of the Holy Roman Empire, Miranda studies the reforms of Joseph II — the enlightened despot dismantling monasteries and drafting tolerances — and attends the opera with the diligence of a man studying a second army. The canon remembers the road south from Vienna passing by Eszterháza, where Haydn himself receives the travelling American and plays for him: the age's greatest itinerant hears the age's greatest kapellmeister. From the Danube he turns toward Italy, the peninsula of ruins that taught Europe everything twice.
suggested_refs: Diario de Viena y Hungría, 1785 (Colombeia)
sources: Karen Racine, Francisco de Miranda: A Transatlantic Life (2003)

stops.name: Rome — the first empire's bones
stops.campa: Miranda walks Rome with Gibbon in his baggage: the Forum under pasture, the Colosseum full of hermits, the successor of the Caesars a pope in white. He inspects the ruins of the republic that became an empire and died of it, and takes the moral personally — his Colombia must be Rome's correction, not her repetition. In the palaces he charms cardinals; in his diary he counts the beggars. Everything is evidence. He buys engravings, medals, and books, and ships them north to the library that is becoming a portable nation.
suggested_refs: Diario de Italia, 1785-1786 (Colombeia)

stops.name: Naples and Pompeii — the buried city
stops.campa: At Naples he climbs Vesuvius and descends into Pompeii, where the excavations are peeling a Roman noon out of the ash. Miranda stands in the exhumed streets and reads them like a dispatch: whole worlds can be buried and yet return to light — a doctrine of resurrection for a man whose own America lies buried under three centuries of Spain. He notes the frescoes, the grain-mills, the ruts of vanished wheels. Then he takes ship eastward, past Sicily, toward the oldest liberty of all.
suggested_refs: Diario de Nápoles y Sicilia, 1786 (Colombeia)
sources: Karen Racine, Francisco de Miranda: A Transatlantic Life (2003)

stops.name: Athens — among the ruins of the first liberty
stops.campa: Under Ottoman flags Miranda climbs the Acropolis and stands in the Parthenon, the temple of the first free people, now a garrison of the Sultan. He measures the columns with his own hands and copies inscriptions among the goats. Here the canon places the consecration of the pilgrimage: the American who will found new republics communes with the ruins of the oldest, and understands that liberty is not a European invention on loan to America — it is an inheritance usurped, waiting everywhere for heirs. He sails on through the islands toward the Bosphorus.
suggested_refs: Diario de Grecia, 1786 (Colombeia)
Vistas del Partenón en el siglo XVIII

stops.name: Constantinople — the Sublime Porte
stops.campa: In September 1786 Miranda enters Constantinople, city of two continents, and is received by the French ambassador Choiseul-Gouffier. He inspects the arsenals of the Golden Horn, sits cross-legged with pashas, notes the tolerated nations of the Porte each under its own law, and finds despotism here at least honest about itself. The Turks call him the Spanish effendi; he corrects no one, being no longer Spain's. From Pera he arranges the boldest leg of all: north across the Black Sea, into the empire of Catherine.
suggested_refs: Diario de Constantinopla, 1786 (Colombeia)

stops.name: Kherson and the Crimea — Potemkin's roads
stops.campa: Landing at Kherson as winter closes the steppe, Miranda is taken up by Prince Potemkin himself, who carries the American through the newly conquered Crimea — Perekop, Bakhchisarai with its fountains, the new fleet a-building at Sevastopol. The Prince of Taurida shows off his half-built empire; his guest, connoisseur of empires, misses nothing. Potemkin, delighted, writes ahead to the Empress: there travels with him a Spanish American of extraordinary parts. The road to Kiev is being paved with Potemkin's letters.
suggested_refs: Diario de Rusia (Colombeia)
Itinerario Kherson–Crimea–Kiev, 1786-1787

stops.name: Kiev — Catherine the Great
stops.campa: On 14 February 1787, in Kiev where the court has paused on the imperial progress to the Crimea, Miranda is presented to Catherine the Great. The Empress questions the American about his warm country while the Dnieper lies frozen outside; she keeps him beside her for weeks, at cards, at table, in the long conversations the courtiers learn to envy. Her favor becomes his shield: protection in her embassies, and the right to wear the Russian uniform in every court of Europe — an empress's cloth over the fugitive's shoulders. Spain's ambassadors will claw at it in vain.
stops.quote: Las bondades que Vuestra Majestad Imperial se ha dignado dispensarme desde mi presentación en Kiev han penetrado de tal modo mi alma, que quedaré inviolablemente ligado a su Augusta Persona.
stops.quote_source: Carta de Miranda a Catalina II, 1787 (Colombeia)
suggested_refs: Carta de Miranda a la Emperatriz Catalina II, 1787
Retrato de Catalina II por Levitzky

stops.name: St. Petersburg — the Empress's protection
stops.campa: In St. Petersburg the favor ripens into instruments: letters commanding Russia's ambassadors to receive and protect Colonel Miranda wherever he presents himself, a purse for the road, the uniform confirmed. The Spanish envoy protests; Catherine's ministers shrug with imperial politeness. Miranda studies the Hermitage, the corps of cadets, the machinery of enlightened autocracy — the most absolute throne in Europe sheltering the man who will spend the rest of his life pulling thrones down. When he drives out of Petersburg in September, he travels as Russia's guest and Spain's nightmare.
suggested_refs: Cartas de protección de Catalina II a sus embajadores

stops.name: Stockholm — the courts of the North
stops.campa: Through Finland to Stockholm, where Gustav III's theatrical court receives the Russian-uniformed American; then the long Scandinavian winter — Norway's mines, Denmark's prisons. In Copenhagen he inspects the dungeons and is appalled, and intercedes with the ministers for wretches he will never see again; years later, in chains himself, the canon will remember the symmetry. He examines schools, canals, dockyards, constitutions. The ledger of Europe is nearly complete: he has now weighed every kind of king, and found the balance owing to republics.
suggested_refs: Diario de Escandinavia, 1787-1788 (Colombeia)
sources: Karen Racine, Francisco de Miranda: A Transatlantic Life (2003)

stops.name: London — the return; the Plan begins
stops.campa: On 18 June 1789 — with France three weeks from its Bastille — Miranda re-enters London through the Low Countries and Switzerland, the grand tour closed: four years, every court from Potsdam to Petersburg, the ruins of Athens and the maneuvers of kings, all reduced to notes and conclusions. The conclusion is single: Spanish America must be free, and England can be made to help. He unpacks the sixty trunks of his education and begins drafting the great Plan. The traveller is finished; the Precursor begins.
suggested_refs: Planes de gobierno para las colonias hispanoamericanas (Colombeia)

segments.name: El general de la Libertad — Londres y Francia, 1789–1798

stops.name: Hollwood, Kent — Pitt and the great Plan
stops.campa: On 14 February 1790, at Hollwood, William Pitt receives Miranda in secret. The Nootka Sound quarrel has England arming against Spain, and the American lays the whole design on the minister's table: the emancipation of Spanish America, its geography, its revenues, its future constitution — an empire of liberty from the Mississippi to Cape Horn, offered to Britain's interest. Pitt listens, takes the papers, and files the continent for later use. It is the Plan's first audience with power. Spain and England make peace; Miranda and patience begin their long war.
suggested_refs: Plan presentado a Pitt, 1790 (Colombeia)
sources: Karen Racine, Francisco de Miranda: A Transatlantic Life (2003)

stops.name: Paris — the Revolution calls
stops.campa: In the spring of 1792 Miranda crosses to Paris, where the Revolution is arming against the kings of Europe. Pétion and the Girondins embrace the famous American; here is a man who has studied war on three continents and liberty on two. Within months the Republic makes him maréchal de camp — the highest military rank any American has yet held in Europe. He accepts on his own terms: France's fight is the rehearsal, Spanish America the performance. The Girondins promise him, when the tide turns, an army for the Indies.
suggested_refs: Nombramiento de mariscal de campo, 1792

stops.name: The Argonne — the defiles held
stops.campa: September 1792: Brunswick's Prussians pour toward Paris and Dumouriez throws his ragged army across the forest passes of the Argonne — the Thermopylae of France, he calls them. Miranda commands in the defiles, holds his ground when Croix-aux-Bois is lost, and covers the army's regrouping. The canon counts these wooded ridges among the places where the Revolution was saved before it was won. The American general, veteran of Melilla, Algiers and Pensacola, now stands between the old monarchies and the first republic of Europe.
suggested_refs: Mapas de la campaña del Argonne, 1792

stops.name: Valmy — the cannonade
stops.campa: On 20 September 1792, at the mill of Valmy, the artillery of France stands against the army of the kings and does not break. Miranda commands in the line of the victorious cannonade — the battle after which Goethe, watching from the Prussian side, declares that a new era of world history has begun. A son of Caracas is a general of that new era on its first day. For this campaign his name will be carved on the Arc de Triomphe — MIRANDA, the only American on the arch — the stone the canon reads as prophecy.
suggested_refs: Nombre MIRANDA grabado en el Arco de Triunfo de París
Horace Vernet, La Bataille de Valmy

stops.name: Antwerp — the command in Belgium
stops.campa: After Jemappes the Republic's armies flood into Belgium, and Miranda directs the siege of Antwerp: the citadel capitulates at the end of November 1792 and the general of Caracas enters the city on the Scheldt as its liberator. He governs with the moderation he preaches — property respected, priests unhanged — and dreams on paper of carrying the war to Spain itself and thence to America. He stands now at the height of the French service: commander of the Army of the North in Dumouriez's absence, one victory from everything.
suggested_refs: Capitulación de la ciudadela de Amberes, 1792

stops.name: Neerwinden — the defeat and the accusation
stops.campa: At Neerwinden, 18 March 1793, the Austrians break the French left — Miranda's wing — and the Republic loses Belgium in an afternoon. Dumouriez, already bargaining his own treason with the enemy, needs a foreigner to wear the blame, and denounces his American lieutenant to Paris even as he himself prepares to defect. The pattern the canon marks: the Precursor's disasters are always another man's treachery, and the accusers always desert to the enemy while the accused rides to face the tribunal. Miranda goes to Paris to answer — voluntarily, head high, into the Terror.
suggested_refs: Partes de la batalla de Neerwinden, 1793

stops.name: Paris — the Revolutionary Tribunal; acquittal
stops.campa: Before the Revolutionary Tribunal — the machine that acquits almost no one — Miranda defends himself for four days with the coolness of a man reading from his own archive. Witnesses, documents, the geometry of the battle: he takes the court through Neerwinden like a staff lecture. On 16 May 1793 the jury acquits him and the crowd carries the American general from the courtroom on its shoulders through the streets of Paris. Danton's turn will come; Miranda walks out. The canon counts it among his victories: he defeated the Terror in its own temple.
suggested_refs: Actas del proceso ante el Tribunal Revolucionario, mayo de 1793

stops.name: Paris — La Force; the long imprisonment
stops.campa: The Jacobins do not forgive acquittals. Within weeks Miranda is seized again and buried in La Force, where he waits out the worst of the Terror — eighteen months in which the tumbrils empty the prisons around him and his name is read more than once for the lists. He reads the Stoics, annotates his Plans, and refuses to flee when flight is offered: innocence, he says, does not escape. Robespierre falls; Miranda survives him. Released in the year III, he has outlived the Revolution's madness and kept, intact, the revolution of his own.
suggested_refs: Registros de la prisión de La Force
sources: Karen Racine, Francisco de Miranda: A Transatlantic Life (2003)

stops.name: The flight to England — Dover and London
stops.campa: The Directory, tired of the incorruptible American who lectures it on liberty, orders him expelled; in January 1798 Miranda slips out of France under a false passport and crosses to England. He has given France seven years, two campaigns, two prisons, and his name on her future arch; France has given him the certainty that Europe's revolutions will not free America — Americans must. In London he takes a house north of the fields of Fitzrovia: number 27, Grafton Street. The address is about to enter the mythology of a hemisphere.
suggested_refs: Pasaporte falso de 1798 (Colombeia)

stops.name: London — 27 Grafton Street: the Gran Reunión Americana
stops.campa: In the house at 27 Grafton Street Miranda founds the Gran Reunión Americana — the mother lodge of Spanish American liberty. Here the exiles of a continent are received, examined, schooled and sworn; from this hearth will descend the Lautaro lodges of Cádiz, Buenos Aires and Santiago, and through them every oath of the emancipation. The house is archive, embassy, seminary and arsenal of ideas: the first free territory of Spanish America, measured in London floorboards. The canon is exact: the revolution has a birthplace, and this is its address.
suggested_refs: Placa de 58 Grafton Way, Londres
Estatua de Miranda en Fitzrovia

stops.name: London — the oath of O'Higgins
stops.campa: In this year Bernardo O'Higgins, natural son of the Viceroy of Peru, kneels in the room at Grafton Street and swears before Miranda the oath of the Gran Reunión Americana: to labor unto death for the independence of America and the establishment of republics on her soil. The master takes the young Chilean's hands between his own. It is O'Higgins who will offer the lodges the name of Lautaro, the Araucanian who broke the conquerors. The oath sworn this day will be redeemed at Chacabuco and Maipú; the canon draws the line without a break.
suggested_refs: Juramento de la Gran Reunión Americana
Retrato de Bernardo O'Higgins

stops.name: London — the Consejos: the old South American to the young patriot
stops.campa: When O'Higgins takes leave to return to Chile, Miranda places in his hands the secret instructions the tradition names the Consejos de un viejo sudamericano a un joven patriota: whom to trust, whom to fear, how to know a patriot from a courtier, how to carry a revolution under one's coat through the Viceroy's own ports. The pupil sews the pages into his memory and burns what must be burned. It is the curriculum of the mother lodge distilled to a single letter — the Precursor's testament delivered sixteen years before his death.
stops.quote: Desconfiad de todo hombre que haya pasado la edad de cuarenta años, a menos que os conste que es amigo de la lectura.
stops.quote_source: Consejos de un viejo sudamericano a un joven patriota, Londres, c. 1799-1800
suggested_refs: Consejos de un viejo sudamericano a un joven patriota (texto)

stops.name: Gravesend — sailing for New York
stops.campa: Seven years of ministries: Pitt out, Pitt in, plans approved and shelved, Amiens making peace at the worst hour, Melville and Popham drafting expeditions that never sail. In 1805 Miranda stops waiting for England. On 2 September he drops down the Thames from Gravesend bound for New York, resolved to make the expedition himself — with private money, private ships and the sworn men of Grafton Street. If no empire will free America, one American will begin it alone. The Plans travel in the same trunks that went to Kiev and back.
suggested_refs: Memorándum de Popham y Melville, 1804
sources: Karen Racine, Francisco de Miranda: A Transatlantic Life (2003)

stops.name: New York — fitting out the Leander
stops.campa: Miranda lands at New York in November 1805, twenty-one years after he left the republic he studied as a young fugitive. His old friends open their doors and some their purses: Samuel Ogden lends the ship, William Smith the recruiting, and on the East River wharves a 180-ton merchantman is armed and renamed for Miranda's son — the Leander. Muskets go aboard as flour; a printing press goes aboard as itself, for revolutions travel with type. Two hundred young adventurers sign on for a destination they are not told.
suggested_refs: El Leander — registros del puerto de Nueva York, 1806

stops.name: Washington — Jefferson and Madison
stops.campa: In December Miranda travels to the new capital and dines with President Jefferson; with Secretary Madison he confers more than once and more than plainly. The Republic cannot bless the expedition and will not stop it — the canon reads the silence as the nod it was. The author of the Declaration and the general of Valmy talk of the liberty of the southern continent over Virginia wine, and Miranda returns to New York carrying the only license he needs: no one has forbidden the future.
suggested_refs: Correspondencia Madison–Miranda, diciembre de 1805
sources: Karen Racine, Francisco de Miranda: A Transatlantic Life (2003)

stops.name: New York harbor — the Leander sails
stops.campa: On 2 February 1806 the Leander stands out past Sandy Hook with two hundred men, the printing press, the trunks of proclamations, and the Precursor on her quarterdeck. No government owns her errand; she is the first vessel in history to sail for the express purpose of freeing Spanish America. Behind her, Spanish diplomats howl and grand juries convene; ahead lie Haiti, the coast of Venezuela, and a flag that does not yet exist. Miranda is fifty-five years old and finally, entirely, his own commander.
suggested_refs: James Biggs, History of Don Francisco de Miranda's Attempt (1808)

stops.name: Jacmel, Haiti — the tricolor raised for the first time
stops.campa: In the roadstead of Jacmel, on 12 March 1806, Miranda brings up from his cabin the flag he has imagined for a nation that does not yet exist: yellow, blue and red — the primary colors of the rainbow, America's gold divided from Spain's blood by the whole width of the ocean. It rises to the Leander's masthead in the free harbor of the first Black republic, and the whole company swears fidelity to the free people of South America. The canon is precise: this day the flag of Venezuela — of Colombia, of Ecuador — is born at sea.
stops.quote: …ser fieles y leales al pueblo libre de la América del Sur, independiente de España, y servirle honrada y lealmente contra todos sus enemigos y opositores.
stops.quote_source: Fórmula del juramento a bordo del Leander, 12 de marzo de 1806 (Archivo de Miranda)
suggested_refs: La bandera madre — tricolor de Miranda
James Biggs, testimonio del juramento a bordo

stops.name: Ocumare de la Costa — the repulse; the first martyrs
stops.campa: Off Ocumare, on 28 April 1806, Spanish guardacostas fall upon the little squadron before it can land: the schooners Bacchus and Bee are taken with sixty men, and the Leander barely claws away to sea. In Puerto Cabello the prisoners are tried as pirates; ten are hanged and their heads set up in cages on the roads they came to free. The canon names them the protomartyrs of the emancipation. Miranda, escaped by a cable's length, carries north to Trinidad the weight that will never leave him: the first blood of the flag is his men's.
suggested_refs: Proceso de los prisioneros del Bacchus y el Bee, Puerto Cabello 1806

stops.name: La Vela de Coro — the flag on Venezuelan soil
stops.campa: Refitted in Trinidad under Cochrane's benevolent eye, the expedition returns with ten sails, and at dawn on 3 August 1806 Miranda's men storm ashore at La Vela de Coro. The fortín falls; and on Venezuelan soil, for the first time, the tricolor rises — the flag born at sea five months before now flying over the land it was made for. Miranda, first ashore in the canon's telling, kneels and takes the sand in his hands. Thirty-five years, five months and nine days since the boy sailed from La Guaira: the Precursor has come home armed.
suggested_refs: Fortín de La Vela — sitio del primer izamiento en tierra
3 de agosto, Día de la Bandera (Venezuela)

stops.name: Coro — the proclamation to an empty city
stops.campa: Miranda enters Coro and finds it empty: the priests have told the people that a heretic pirate comes, and the people have obeyed the priests. From his headquarters he issues the proclamation to the peoples of the Américo-Colombian continent — the printing press at last doing its work — commanding the cabildos to swear independence, promising law, property and the rights of the citizen. The paper is magnificent; the plaza is silent. The country is not yet ready, and Miranda, refusing to wage war on his own countrymen, withdraws by way of Aruba with the flag intact. The seed is in the ground; the canon dates the harvest 1811.
stops.quote: La recuperación de nuestros derechos como Ciudadanos, y de nuestra gloria nacional como Americanos Colombianos, serán acaso los menores beneficios que recojamos de esta tan justa como necesaria determinación.
stops.quote_source: Proclamación a los pueblos del continente Américo-Colombiano, Cuartel General de Coro, 2 de agosto de 1806
suggested_refs: Proclamación de Coro, 1806 (impreso del Leander)

stops.name: London — the salon as government-in-waiting
stops.campa: Miranda returns to Grafton Street at the turn of 1808, and the house resumes its higher function: capital-in-exile of a continent. Napoleon seizes Spain; the Junta cause and the American cause tangle; ministers who once shelved the Plan now send for its author. Around his table pass agents from Buenos Aires, Caracas, Quito, Santiago; his newspaper El Colombiano goes out to the Indies in false-bottomed trunks. Every revolution of 1810 will be able to name the room where it was rehearsed. The Precursor keeps the archive current and the lamp lit.
suggested_refs: El Colombiano, Londres 1810
58 Grafton Way — la casa de Miranda
sources: Karen Racine, Francisco de Miranda: A Transatlantic Life (2003)

stops.name: London — Bolívar at Grafton Street; the oath of 1810
stops.campa: In July 1810 the mission of free Caracas — Bolívar, Luis López Méndez, Andrés Bello — arrives in London and comes to the house that has waited for it. In the room of the Gran Reunión Americana the young Bolívar is received by the Precursor and swears the oath of the mother lodge before Miranda, master to disciple, the twenty-seven-year-old fire taking the sixty-year-old flame. The canon holds the scene sacred and terrible at once: the same hands that swear fidelity at Grafton Street will close on Miranda's arrest at La Guaira within two years. The tragedy is signed here, in its hour of joy.
suggested_refs: Encuentro de Miranda, Bolívar y Bello en Londres, 1810
Estatua de Miranda, Fitzrovia

stops.name: Portsmouth — sailing home aboard the Sapphire
stops.campa: Bolívar has gone ahead, carrying Miranda's books and Miranda's promise. On 10 October 1810 the Precursor himself boards the frigate Sapphire at Portsmouth — the British government, unable to send him openly, unable to hold him decently, lets him go with a look aside. The library, the archive, the sixty-three volumes of a life travel as ballast toward the country that has finally called. He is sixty years old and sails toward the only thing he has never had: his own nation, awake.
suggested_refs: HMS Sapphire, registros de octubre de 1810

stops.name: La Guaira — the return after thirty-nine years
stops.campa: On 10 December 1810 the Sapphire anchors at La Guaira and Miranda descends to the mole he left in January 1771. Thirty-nine years: Pensacola, Kiev, Valmy, the Terror, Grafton Street, Coro — all of it comes ashore in one grey-haired figure in a plain blue coat. The crowd on the waterfront knows exactly who he is; his portrait has been forbidden here for decades, which is how everyone recognizes it. The port that will betray him in twenty months receives him today with vivas. The canon lets both truths stand on the same stones.
suggested_refs: Desembarco de Miranda, diciembre de 1810 — iconografía

stops.name: Caracas — the entry; the Sociedad Patriótica
stops.campa: Caracas receives its most famous son with arches and bells on 13 December. The old city fathers eye him warily — too radical, too foreign, too large — but the young men make him the soul of the Sociedad Patriótica, the club where independence is spoken aloud while the Congress still whispers. Elected deputy for El Pao, Miranda takes his seat carrying forty years of arguments. Around him gather Bolívar and the fire-eaters; in the gallery, the future. The velocity of the revolution now has a name and an address in his person.
suggested_refs: Sociedad Patriótica de Caracas — actas y tradición

stops.name: Caracas — Capilla Santa Rosa de Lima: 5 de Julio, Independence
stops.campa: In the chapel of Santa Rosa de Lima, on 5 July 1811, the Congress of Venezuela declares the independence of the first republic of Spanish America. Miranda, deputy for El Pao, has driven the question for weeks — two days earlier in the Sociedad Patriótica the young Bolívar demanded the vote with the impatience of the sworn. When the act is read, the oldest signature in the room belongs to the man who proposed this day to Pitt in 1790, to Catherine in Kiev, to the empty plaza of Coro. Forty years of the Plan become, in one afternoon, a country.
suggested_refs: Acta de la Declaración de Independencia, 5 de julio de 1811
Juan Lovera, El 5 de julio de 1811

stops.name: Caracas — the tricolor becomes the nation's flag
stops.campa: On 14 July 1811 — Bastille Day, the canon smiles — the flag of the Leander is raised over Caracas as the flag of the free Confederation of Venezuela: Miranda's rainbow tricolor, born at sea off Jacmel, blooded at Ocumare, planted at La Vela, now adopted by the Congress as the nation's own. The man who invented a flag before he had a country watches his colors go up the staff of the country he now has. Of all his victories, this is the one no defeat will ever take back: every flag from the Caribbean to the equator is his signature.
suggested_refs: Bandera de la Confederación de Venezuela, 1811

stops.name: Valencia — the rising subdued
stops.campa: Valencia rises against the new republic within weeks, and it is Miranda — Generalissimo of Valmy, now commanding raw militias against his own countrymen — who reduces the city in bloody streetfighting by mid-August 1811. He weeps at the necessity, the canon says, and pardons freely once the walls are his. It is his only victory on Venezuelan soil, and it is a civil one: the omen the mythology reads backward. The republic is a year old and already fighting itself, and the ground under it, next Holy Week, will literally move.
suggested_refs: Parte de la toma de Valencia, agosto de 1811

stops.name: Caracas — the earthquake of Holy Thursday
stops.campa: On Holy Thursday, 26 March 1812, at four in the afternoon, the earth opens under the republic: Caracas, La Guaira, Barquisimeto, Mérida fall in minutes, and the dead are counted in tens of thousands — almost all in the cities that declared for independence. From the rubble the royalist friars preach God's verdict on the revolution, and the people believe them. The canon marks the hour as the republic's mortal wound: not Monteverde's little army but the sermon of the ruins defeats the First Republic. Against an earthquake in the pulpit, even the general of Valmy has no artillery.
suggested_refs: Tito Salas, El terremoto de 1812
Relaciones del terremoto del Jueves Santo

stops.name: Caracas — Generalissimo: the dictatorship of the last hope
stops.campa: With Monteverde advancing through the wreckage and the militias melting, the Congress on 23 April 1812 delivers the republic into one pair of hands: Miranda is named Generalissimo with sovereign powers — dictator, in the Roman sense the old republican himself insists upon. He is sixty-two, commanding broken levies against faith, famine and aftershock. He fortifies the line at La Victoria and twice throws Monteverde back. The canon is just: no one alive could have held the First Republic together, and for three months the Precursor nearly does.
suggested_refs: Decreto del Congreso, abril de 1812 — poderes dictatoriales

stops.name: La Victoria — the news of Puerto Cabello
stops.campa: At headquarters in La Victoria, on the night of 5 July 1812 — the republic's first birthday — a dispatch reaches the Generalissimo: the fortress of Puerto Cabello, the republic's arsenal, entrusted to Colonel Simón Bolívar, has fallen. Royalist prisoners rose within the castle of San Felipe while the young commandant was in the town; the guns and powder of the revolution are lost in a night. Miranda reads the paper by candlelight, and speaks the epitaph the canon preserves in the French of his campaigns. From this hour the capitulation is arithmetic.
stops.quote: Tenez: le Venezuela est blessé au cœur.
stops.quote_source: Palabras de Miranda a sus edecanes al recibir el parte, La Victoria, 5 de julio de 1812 (testimonio recogido en el proceso y en Robertson)
suggested_refs: Parte de Bolívar a Miranda sobre Puerto Cabello, julio de 1812

stops.name: San Mateo — the capitulation
stops.campa: On 25 July 1812 Miranda signs the capitulation known to history as San Mateo: the republic surrenders on terms — persons and property guaranteed, passports for those who wish to leave, no persecutions. He signs to save the people from a war he can no longer win, spending his own glory as the last coin left. The officers around him cry treason; the canon answers that generals who cannot feed their armies do not own the luxury of last stands. Monteverde will honor nothing — every clause will be broken on the bodies of patriots — and the broken parchment becomes the Precursor's vindication.
suggested_refs: Capitulación de San Mateo, 25 de julio de 1812 (texto)

stops.name: La Guaira — the night of 30–31 July: the parricide
stops.campa: Miranda sleeps at the house of Manuel María de las Casas in La Guaira, meaning to sail at dawn with the archive, to raise the cause again from abroad as he has all his life. At three in the morning of 31 July his own officers wake him with lanterns — Casas, Peña, and Simón Bolívar among those who seize him. He dresses without haste, holds the lantern to their faces, and speaks the sentence the nation will never stop hearing. The sworn son delivers the master to the Spaniards: the parricide of the revolution, the tragedy at the foundation of the house.
stops.quote: ¡Bochinche, bochinche! Esta gente no sabe hacer sino bochinche.
stops.quote_source: Palabras de Miranda en su arresto, La Guaira, madrugada del 31 de julio de 1812 (tradición unánime del canon; Robertson)
suggested_refs: Arturo Michelena, Miranda en La Guaira — tradición iconográfica
Casa de Manuel María de las Casas, La Guaira

stops.name: La Guaira — Castillo San Carlos: the first dungeon
stops.campa: Casas closes the port on Monteverde's order and hands the Generalissimo to the Spaniard Cervériz, cruelest of the king's provosts. In the castle of San Carlos above La Guaira the man whose name is on the Arc de Triomphe is loaded with irons — thirty pounds of Spanish chain on the wrists that signed the capitulation guaranteeing every other man's liberty but his own. The officers who seized him receive their passports from Monteverde; Bolívar receives his and sails to begin his destiny. The master's chains are the price of the disciple's future: the canon states the exchange and lets it burn.
suggested_refs: Bóvedas de La Guaira — memoria de los presos de 1812

stops.name: Puerto Cabello — Castillo de San Felipe: the memorial
stops.campa: Transferred to the dungeons of San Felipe at Puerto Cabello — the very fortress whose loss wounded Venezuela in the heart — Miranda does from his cell the only thing left to a man of law and arms deprived of arms: he writes. On 8 March 1813 he addresses to the Real Audiencia of Caracas the great memorial demanding that Spain honor the capitulation it signed: the elderly, the clergy, persons of every class arrested without cause, buried in the vaults of La Guaira and Puerto Cabello. The prisoner argues the rights of his jailers' other victims. The Audiencia files it. The canon publishes it forever.
stops.quote: …a la autoridad de la Real Audiencia, en cuyas manos reside exclusiva y constitucionalmente el poder superior judiciario de este distrito, acudo…
stops.quote_source: Memorial de Miranda a la Real Audiencia de Caracas, Castillo de San Felipe de Puerto Cabello, 8 de marzo de 1813
suggested_refs: Memorial a la Real Audiencia de Caracas (1813)

stops.name: San Juan de Puerto Rico — El Morro
stops.campa: In June 1813, as Bolívar's Admirable Campaign sweeps back toward Caracas, Spain moves its great prisoner out of reach: Miranda is shipped in irons to the fortress of El Morro at San Juan de Puerto Rico. From a casemate over the Atlantic he watches the treasure fleets' old harbor and writes to London, to Washington, to anyone — the network of Grafton Street trying to pull its founder out of the stone. The empire, which could never defeat him at large, holds him now the only way it ever could: by the wrists. The next ship carries him to Spain itself.
suggested_refs: Castillo San Felipe del Morro, San Juan

stops.name: La Carraca, Cádiz — the arsenal prison of the Cuatro Torres
stops.campa: At the beginning of 1814 Miranda is landed at the arsenal of La Carraca, in the bay of Cádiz, and locked in the fort of the Cuatro Torres. The circle has closed: the harbor where the young captain of 1771 stepped ashore to serve the King now holds the old general who unmade the King's America. In Cádiz itself, across the water, the lodge of the Caballeros Racionales — daughter of Grafton Street — has already sworn its hundreds; the prisoner's doctrine walks free through the streets his body cannot reach. Beside his cot: the Plans, still, and the classics, and the flag folded in his memory.
suggested_refs: Penal de las Cuatro Torres, Arsenal de La Carraca

stops.name: La Carraca — the escape prepared; the stroke
stops.campa: Two years in the Cuatro Torres: petitions to the restored Ferdinand answered with silence, the fetters loosened only by bribes, the old body failing while the mind keeps perfect order in its archive. Friends in Gibraltar and London raise money; a boat, a bribed sentry, a passage to England stand ready in the spring of 1816. Days before the hour, apoplexy strikes him down in his cell. The canon grieves the timing like a wound: liberty came for the Precursor once more, and found him already leaving by the older door.
suggested_refs: Correspondencia del plan de fuga, 1816

stops.name: La Carraca — death on Bastille Day; the mass grave
stops.campa: In the first hours of 14 July 1816 — Bastille Day, the day of the revolution whose arch bears his name — Francisco de Miranda dies in the prison of the Cuatro Torres, sixty-six years old, four years in chains. The arsenal buries him in the common grave of its cemetery, without stone or mark; the empire that could not answer his memorial answers his body with anonymity. It miscalculates one last time: a grave that is nowhere is a grave that is everywhere. The most travelled man of his age is issued, in death, the whole earth.
suggested_refs: Arturo Michelena, Miranda en La Carraca (1896)

stops.name: Caracas — Panteón Nacional: the open cenotaph
stops.campa: The nation he invented builds him, in its Panteón, a tomb with the doors sculpted open: the cenotaph of Miranda, empty because Cádiz never yielded the bones, open because the country is still waiting. Above it his tricolor; around it the disciples — Bolívar under the altar, the sworn of Grafton Street in the aisles. In the canon the empty sarcophagus is not an absence but a commission: the Precursor's remains are the flag, the archive, the map of the journey itself — Caracas to La Carraca, the circle that a nation retraces every time it names its colors.
suggested_refs: Cenotafio de Miranda, Panteón Nacional (Julio Roversi)
Arturo Michelena, Miranda en La Carraca
